about.title: About
paragraphs: I build software for people who are already in the middle of something else. At Siali that something is a factory floor. I decide what the product is for, and I build it: the interface, the system behind it, and what keeps it running. If those parts do not agree, the person on the floor makes the wrong call. I live in Cantabria and work from here.

How a thing looks and what it is for are easy to split and hard to keep together. A screen can be finished and still be useless. I would rather take a part away than explain it. The shape of the data usually decides the shape of the screen, so I treat them as the same decision.
I also keep a small product for one football academy. Staff and players use it. It has to be obvious on a tired evening. That is the brief I trust.

rely.thesis: Factories use Rely to check every part on the line. Operators need a verdict they can read at a glance. Engineers need to set up what gets checked and train the models behind it. I designed and built the frontend for both.
rely.result: Rely monitors factories worldwide. If it fails, the line stops and the client loses hundreds of thousands of euros. Siali took on the complex projects other companies rejected.

leadership.title: How I lead
leadership.content: I assigned and monitored work for around 10 interns and two frontend developers. I designed their tests and training, and decided who stayed.

decisions.title: Rely first: production and training stay in sync
decisions.content:
Rely runs on the line. Rely Cloud is where we label images and train the models. Some clients have no Rely Cloud, some run it on their own servers, some use it in the cloud, and some are custom projects with their own interfaces. I had to design one link that worked for all of them.

I decided production leads: you don't think about the cloud until you use the line. A station is one inspection point on the line. When you create one in Rely, its project in Rely Cloud is created too. A station has recipes, and a recipe is usually one part reference, with its own cameras, models and decisions for the PLC, camera or robot arm. Each recipe has views, one per side of the part, seen by one or more cameras while a robot arm turns it. Each view gets its own dataset and is trained on its own, because defects differ from one side to another.

All of this is created and linked automatically. Parts that pass the line land in the right dataset. In Rely Cloud people label them, by hand or with a model's predictions, train, and the new models show up already linked to their recipes. The user just sees things appear.

To get there I designed for the edge cases: users without the link key, and users who don't want Rely to lead. Rely first can be switched off, and a settings screen maps views to datasets by hand.

The loop closes in production. While reviewing parts the model has already judged, the user picks images to relabel and sends them to that view's dataset, another one or a new one. The labelling happens in Rely Cloud, and they choose whether it syncs back.

decisions.title: Engineers build the inspection themselves
decisions.content: We used to write a Python script for each line. I replaced it with a visual editor. The engineer connects blocks for the trigger, the cameras, the detection model and the rule that decides OK or KO, then publishes it to the station. Blocks are named after things they already know, like a camera or a PLC.

decisions.title: Showing which recipe is running
decisions.content: As stations and recipes multiplied, people lost track of which recipe was running on each line. A small "live" badge wasn't enough. I replaced it with a production slot: the active recipe plugs into it like a cartridge into a game console.

loadzone.thesis: Coaching staff need to know who is ready to train before the session starts, and players have to answer quickly for that to work. I design and build Loadzone alone.
loadzone.cromoCaption: The Streak Cromo on the player's phone. Tilt it to see the foil. It's the reward for answering.

decisions.title: The whole squad on one screen
decisions.content: Before and after each session, staff check every player's recovery, energy, soreness, sleep and post-session effort (RPE). If a player hasn't answered, the cell shows a dash, so nobody mistakes a gap for a good score. Colour marks who needs attention first.

decisions.title: One question at a time
decisions.content: Players answer before and after the session. Each screen asks one thing, with large text and a slider big enough for a thumb. A counter shows how many are left. The card appears only once they finish.

decisions.title: Sessions built from drills
decisions.content: Staff build a session by placing drills on it. Each drill has a duration, pitch size and number of players, plus a tactical type picked from a list. Dropdowns keep it quick and consistent.
